title: How do idempotent producers help achieve exactly-once semantics, and why does it matter?
shortTitle: How idempotent producers help achieve exactly-once semantics, and why it matters

s1_definition.profdef: An idempotent producer is the foundation of exactly-once semantics on the write side. It guarantees that a record sent once is written exactly once even if the producer retries after a lost acknowledgement, because the broker deduplicates using a producer id and a monotonically increasing per-partition sequence number. Exactly-once semantics end to end then combines this idempotent write with transactional commits and read-committed consumers, so a record is produced once, grouped writes are atomic, and consumers never see duplicates or partial results. Without idempotent producers, retries silently create duplicates and exactly-once is impossible.
s1_definition.analogy: Imagine Rajesh instructs National Bank of India to transfer fifty thousand rupees. The phone line drops before he hears "done," so his app resends. An idempotent producer is like stamping each instruction with a unique serial number: the bank sees the same serial twice and files it only once, so Rajesh is debited exactly once, not twice. That single guarantee is the first brick of exactly-once; stacking transactions and read-committed on top makes the whole money movement happen once and only once.
s1_definition.oneliner: Idempotent producers remove retry duplicates on the write path, which is the essential first building block of end-to-end exactly-once.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** An idempotent producer is the foundation of exactly-once semantics on the write side. It guarantees that a record sent once is written exactly once even if the producer retries after a lost acknowledgement, because the broker deduplicates using a producer id and a monotonically increasing per-partition sequence number. Exactly-once semantics end to end then combines this idempotent write with transactional commits and read-committed consumers, so a record is produced once, grouped writes are atomic, and consumers never see duplicates or partial results. Without idempotent producers, retries silently create duplicates and exactly-once is impossible.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** Imagine Rajesh instructs National Bank of India to transfer fifty thousand rupees. The phone line drops before he hears "done," so his app resends. An idempotent producer is like stamping each instruction with a unique serial number: the bank sees the same serial twice and files it only once, so Rajesh is debited exactly once, not twice. That single guarantee is the first brick of exactly-once; stacking transactions and read-committed on top makes the whole money movement happen once and only once.

**One line to remember:** Idempotent producers remove retry duplicates on the write path, which is the essential first building block of end-to-end exactly-once.

sections.s2_technical:
Start with why duplicates happen at all. A producer sends a record, the broker appends it to the log, but the acknowledgement is lost on the way back. The producer cannot tell whether the write succeeded, so it retries. Without protection, the same record is now in the log twice. In a bank that could mean a duplicate debit, which is a serious correctness failure.

The idempotent producer fixes this at the broker. When idempotence is enabled, the broker gives the producer a unique producer id and the producer attaches a sequence number to each record per partition, increasing by one each time. The broker remembers the last sequence it accepted for that producer and partition. If a retried record carries a sequence that is less than or equal to the last one written, the broker recognizes it as a duplicate, acknowledges it so the producer stops retrying, but does not append it again. If the sequence jumps ahead unexpectedly, the broker raises an out-of-order error, which surfaces a real problem rather than silently corrupting the log.

Enabling it is simple: `enable.idempotence=true`, which is the default in current Kafka. It requires `acks=all` so the record is on all in-sync replicas before acknowledgement, `retries` greater than zero so retrying is possible, and `max.in.flight.requests.per.connection` at most five so the broker can still detect and reorder duplicates correctly.

Now connect it to exactly-once. Exactly-once semantics means each record is processed and its effects applied once, no more and no less. It has three parts. First, the write must not duplicate on retry, which is exactly what the idempotent producer gives you. Second, a group of writes across partitions and topics must be atomic, which the transactional producer adds on top of idempotence. Third, in a consume-process-produce loop, the consumer offsets must be committed in the same transaction as the output, so you never reprocess or skip, and consumers must read with read-committed. The idempotent producer is the base layer; the transaction layer and the isolation level complete the picture.

The senior nuances are these. Idempotence is scoped to a single producer session and per partition. Across a producer restart the producer id changes, so idempotence alone does not dedup across sessions; that is one reason transactions use a stable transactional id to fence zombies and preserve guarantees across restarts. Idempotence does not protect against the application itself choosing to resend different data, nor against duplicate side effects in external systems, so for true end-to-end exactly-once you still design idempotent consumers keyed on a business id. Why it matters in banking is blunt: a duplicated transfer, settlement, or fee is money created or destroyed, so removing retry duplicates is not an optimization, it is a correctness requirement.
sections.s3_banking:
Problem 1 — National Bank of India produces a fee-charge event whenever a trade settles. On a flaky network the producer frequently retries after lost acknowledgements. Without idempotence, some fee events are written twice, and the billing consumer charges Priya the brokerage fee twice. This is exactly the retry-duplicate problem the idempotent producer removes.

Problem 2 — The bank wants exactly-once for the full settle-and-charge flow: read a trade, produce a settlement event and a fee event, and commit the read offset, all atomically. The idempotent producer is the base that makes the writes non-duplicating; the transaction wraps them with the offset commit. This is exactly how the pieces stack into exactly-once.

We simulate the idempotent write path in plain Java. A `ProducerSession` assigns a producer id and increasing sequence numbers; an `IdempotentLog` on the broker side deduplicates by producer id and sequence. We then send a fee event, force two retries, and show the log contains it once. Finally we wrap a settlement plus fee plus offset in a simple transaction wrapper to show the exactly-once composition. The code will show: a `FeeEvent`, a `ProducerSession`, an `IdempotentLog`, a tiny `ExactlyOnceUnit`, and a demo.

```yaml
# application.yml — producer tuned for exactly-once write path
spring:
  kafka:
    bootstrap-servers: localhost:9092
    producer:
      acks: all
      retries: 2147483647
      properties:
        enable.idempotence: true
        max.in.flight.requests.per.connection: 5
      transaction-id-prefix: tx-settle-fee-
    consumer:
      isolation-level: read_committed
      enable-auto-commit: false
```

sections.s5_journey:
Input data: a brokerage fee event for trade TRD-001 that the producer sends and then retries twice, followed by an exactly-once unit around offset 500.

Step 1: The producer session assigns producer id 777 and sequence 0 for partition 2, then sends the fee event. The broker records that the last accepted sequence for producer 777 on partition 2 is 0 and appends the event.

Step 2: The acknowledgement is lost, so the producer retries the identical record with sequence 0. The broker sees 0 is not greater than the last accepted 0, recognizes a duplicate, acknowledges it, and does not append again.

Step 3: The producer retries once more, still sequence 0, and again the broker deduplicates. After all retries the log contains the fee exactly once, so Priya is charged once.

Step 4: For the exactly-once flow, the unit begins at offset 500 and produces a new fee with the next sequence, 1. The idempotent log appends it because 1 is exactly one greater than 0.

Step 5: The unit commits, which advances the processed offset to 500 and makes the write final together. If it had aborted instead, the offset would not advance and the record would be safely reprocessed later without a duplicate, because idempotence and the transaction keep the effect single.

```
2026-10-24 20:50:21 [INFO   ] Retries stored? false/false -> log size=1 (fee charged ONCE)
2026-10-24 20:50:21 [INFO   ] Committed offset=500, total fees in log=2
```
sections.s5b_flow:
```
  Producer (pid=777, seq=0)  send FEE(TRD-001)
    │
    ▼
  Broker IdempotentLog
    │ seq 0 > lastSeq -1 ? yes → WRITE, lastSeq=0
    │ (ack lost) retry seq 0 → 0 <= 0 → ACK, NO write
    │ retry seq 0 again      → 0 <= 0 → ACK, NO write
    ▼
  Log: [FEE TRD-001]  (exactly once)

  Exactly-once consume-process-produce:
  begin(offset=500)
    │ produce FEE(TRD-002) seq=1 (idempotent write)
    ▼
  commit() → offset 500 advanced + write final  TOGETHER
    │  (abort → offset NOT advanced → reprocessed, still once)
    ▼
  read_committed consumers see each fee exactly once
```

sections.s6_takeaway:
Idempotent producers are the foundation of exactly-once semantics because they eliminate the one unavoidable source of duplicates on the write path: retries after a lost acknowledgement. The scenario is simple and common. A producer sends a record, the broker writes it, but the acknowledgement is lost, so the producer retries and, without protection, the record is now in the log twice. With idempotence enabled, the broker gives the producer a unique producer id and the producer stamps each record with an increasing per-partition sequence number. The broker remembers the last sequence it accepted, so a retried record with a sequence it has already seen is acknowledged but not written again. It needs acks all, retries above zero, and at most five in-flight requests, and it is the default in current Kafka.

By itself, the idempotent producer gives exactly-once on a single partition within one producer session. Full end-to-end exactly-once stacks two more things on top. Transactions make a group of writes across partitions and topics atomic, and in a consume-process-produce loop the consumer offsets are committed inside the same transaction as the output, so you never reprocess or skip. Consumers then read with read-committed so they only see committed results. The idempotent producer is the base brick; transactions and read-committed complete the structure.

Why it matters in a bank is not subtle. A duplicated fee, settlement, or transfer is money charged twice or created out of nothing, which is a correctness and compliance failure, not a performance blip. So removing retry duplicates is a hard requirement. I also keep the honest boundaries in mind: idempotence does not dedup across a producer restart because the producer id changes, which is why transactions use a stable transactional id to fence zombies, and it does not protect external side effects, so I still make downstream consumers idempotent on a business id.

In my banking platform at National Bank of India, every producer runs idempotent so a retried brokerage-fee event is never written twice and Priya is never double-charged. For the settle-and-charge flow, we go further: a transactional producer writes the settlement event and the fee event and commits the trade topic's offset in one transaction, and the billing and ledger consumers read with read-committed. The senior framing I give is that idempotent producers are what make the word exactly-once honest on the write side, and they are the non-negotiable first layer on which transactions and isolation build the complete guarantee.
